description: Agonist and antagonist roles in sporting actions and how slow and fast twitch fibres suit different activities.
content_html:
Muscles Work in Opposing Pairs

Muscles can only pull — they cannot push. To produce movement in one direction and then reverse it, muscles work in opposing pairs called antagonistic pairs. In every movement, one muscle contracts to produce the movement (the agonist) while the opposing muscle relaxes and lengthens to allow it (the antagonist).

The roles of agonist and antagonist swap when the movement is reversed. At the elbow: during a bicep curl (elbow flexion) the biceps is the agonist and the triceps is the antagonist. When you straighten your arm back down (elbow extension) the triceps becomes the agonist and the biceps becomes the antagonist. This reciprocal relationship is how smooth, controlled movement is produced.

The Four Key Antagonistic Pairs

You need to know four antagonistic pairs with their specific joint actions.

Biceps and triceps at the elbow: The biceps flexes the elbow (agonist in a rowing pull, a pull-up, a forehand shot in badminton) while the triceps relaxes. To extend the elbow (shot put release, press-up push, javelin throw) the triceps becomes the agonist and the biceps relaxes.

Quadriceps and hamstrings at the knee: The quadriceps extend the knee (agonist in kicking, jumping, the push phase of cycling) while the hamstrings relax. To flex the knee (recovery leg in sprinting, curling the leg in swimming breaststroke kick) the hamstrings become the agonist and the quadriceps relax. The hamstrings are particularly prone to strain when they contract rapidly as the agonist during the late swing phase of sprinting — when they decelerate the extending knee.

Hip flexors and gluteus maximus at the hip: The hip flexors flex the hip (agonist when swinging the leg forward in running) while the gluteus maximus relaxes. When the hip extends — the drive phase pushing the leg backward in running, the downstroke in cycling, the jump in volleyball — the gluteus maximus is the agonist and the hip flexors relax.

Gastrocnemius and tibialis anterior at the ankle: The gastrocnemius plantar-flexes the ankle (agonist in a sprint start, a jump take-off, pointing the foot in gymnastics) while the tibialis anterior relaxes. When dorsi-flexion is needed (heel-strike landing, pulling the foot up in the swing phase of running) the tibialis anterior is the agonist and the gastrocnemius relaxes.

Key Fact

Four antagonistic pairs and their joints: biceps/triceps (elbow), quadriceps/hamstrings (knee), hip flexors/gluteus maximus (hip), gastrocnemius/tibialis anterior (ankle). In each case, the agonist contracts and the antagonist relaxes; roles swap when movement direction reverses.

Students often assume the agonist must always be the bigger, stronger muscle. This is wrong — the agonist is simply whichever muscle is producing the current movement. The tibialis anterior is smaller than the gastrocnemius, but when you dorsi-flex the ankle (pull the foot up) the tibialis anterior is the agonist and the gastrocnemius is the antagonist, regardless of their relative sizes. The key is to anchor your answer to the specific phase of movement described in the question. Exam questions often ask “identify the agonist during the upward phase of a bicep curl” or “name the antagonist when the knee is being extended.” Always start by identifying the movement phase, then name the muscle contracting to produce it as the agonist.

Muscle Fibre Types

Not all muscle fibres are the same. Skeletal muscles contain a mixture of three fibre types with very different properties, and the proportion of each type influences which activities a performer is naturally suited to.

Type I fibres (slow-twitch) contract slowly but are highly resistant to fatigue. They have a rich blood supply, many mitochondria and high levels of myoglobin (the protein that stores oxygen in muscle), which gives them a red colour. They generate force aerobically and can sustain activity for long periods. Marathon runners and professional cyclists have a high proportion of Type I fibres, and activities like long-distance swimming, cross-country running and triathlon rely on them heavily.

Type IIa fibres (fast-twitch oxidative) represent an intermediate option. They contract faster than Type I fibres and produce more force, but they can also use aerobic metabolism when required. They fatigue more quickly than Type I but more slowly than Type IIx. They are dominant in activities requiring a sustained but high effort — 400 m and 800 m running, many team sports such as football and rugby where repeated bursts are interspersed with recovery periods.

Type IIx fibres (fast-twitch glycolytic) are the fastest and most powerful but fatigue very rapidly. They rely almost entirely on anaerobic energy sources (glycogen, phosphocreatine) and have few mitochondria. They are activated only for maximal-intensity, short-duration efforts: 100 m sprinting, shot put, Olympic weightlifting, plyometric jumping. Sprinters like Dina Asher-Smith have a genetic advantage in Type IIx fibre proportion, which contributes to explosive acceleration.

Key Fact

Three fibre types: Type I (slow-twitch, aerobic, fatigue-resistant — marathon); Type IIa (intermediate, aerobic and anaerobic, moderate fatigue — 800 m / team sports); Type IIx (fast-twitch, anaerobic, rapid fatigue — 100 m sprint / weightlifting).

Research suggests that the ratio of Type I to Type II fibres is largely determined by genetics and does not change significantly with training. However, there is some evidence that Type IIx fibres can be converted to Type IIa fibres with prolonged aerobic training, and that resistance training can increase the size (hypertrophy) of both Type II subtypes, increasing their force output. For GCSE purposes, the key point is: fibre type is genetically determined (you choose your parents wisely if you want to be a sprinter), but fibre size and efficiency can be improved through appropriate training. This is why elite sprinters and elite endurance athletes have very different physiological profiles.
exam_tip_html: On questions about antagonistic pairs, always anchor your answer to the specific phase of movement — ‘during elbow flexion’ or ‘during the upward phase.’ The mark scheme distinguishes agonist and antagonist by movement phase, not by anatomy alone. On muscle fibre questions, use the full Edexcel labels: Type I, Type IIa, Type IIx — do not write ‘slow-twitch’ or ‘fast-twitch’ alone as these are informal descriptors. Justify your sport–fibre match with a reason: ‘Type I because the marathon is a prolonged aerobic activity lasting over two hours, requiring fatigue-resistant fibres’ scores more marks than naming the type alone.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • In antagonistic pairs, the agonist contracts to produce a movement while the antagonist relaxes; the four key pairs are biceps/triceps (elbow), quadriceps/hamstrings (knee), hip flexors/gluteus maximus (hip), gastrocnemius/tibialis anterior (ankle).
  • Three muscle fibre types: Type I (slow-twitch, aerobic, endurance), Type IIa (intermediate, aerobic and anaerobic, team sports), Type IIx (fast-twitch, anaerobic, explosive power).
  • The proportion of fibre types is largely genetically determined and influences athletic suitability; training can improve fibre size and efficiency but cannot fundamentally alter the ratio of slow to fast fibres.

practice_questions.text:
During the downward phase of a squat (knee flexion), which muscle is acting as the antagonist?
A) Quadriceps
B) Hamstrings
C) Gastrocnemius
D) Gluteus maximus
practice_questions.marks: A) Quadriceps [1 mark]. During knee flexion the hamstrings are the agonist and the quadriceps are the antagonist.

practice_questions.text: State which muscle fibre type a 100 m sprinter would predominantly use and give one reason why.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: Type IIx. 1 mark for reason: they produce the most explosive, powerful contractions needed for maximal sprint speed / they rely on anaerobic energy, appropriate for the short, high-intensity duration of a 100 m race.

practice_questions.text: Explain the roles of the biceps and triceps when performing a shot put release.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: at the moment of release the elbow is extending. 1 mark for: the triceps is the agonist, contracting to extend the elbow and drive the shot forward. 1 mark for: the biceps is the antagonist, relaxing to allow the extension to occur smoothly.

practice_questions.text:
The table below shows the percentage of Type I muscle fibres in three athletes.

Athlete     | Sport              | % Type I fibres
Felicia     | 1500 m running     | 68%
Gareth      | 100 m sprint       | 24%
Harrison    | Football (midfield)| 51%

Interpret what the data shows about how fibre composition relates to sport demands.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: Felicia has the highest % Type I (68%) consistent with 1500 m being an aerobic endurance event requiring fatigue-resistant fibres (1+1). Gareth has the lowest (24%) consistent with sprinting requiring explosive Type IIx fibres for maximal anaerobic power (1+1). Harrison is intermediate (51%) reflecting football's mixed demands — repeated short sprints (Type II) interspersed with lower-intensity running (Type I) (1). Maximum 4 marks; credit any valid data quote + sporting implication combination.

practice_questions.text: A strength coach argues that knowing an athlete's muscle fibre composition is essential when designing a training programme. Assess this claim, referring to the properties of each fibre type and the implications for programme design.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6): Accurately describes all three fibre types with correct properties. Links each type to specific training methods (e.g. Type IIx benefits from plyometrics and maximal sprint intervals; Type I from continuous aerobic training). Identifies limitation: fibre ratio is largely genetic, so design must work with existing ratio. Reaches a supported judgement (e.g. 'knowing fibre composition is highly useful for setting training emphasis but should not be the only factor as technique, psychology and sport demands also matter'). Consistent sporting application.
Secure (3-4): Describes at least two types accurately with mostly correct links to training. Partial judgement.
Developing (2): Basic description of one or two types; limited training link.
Emerging (1): Simple point about muscles and training with no fibre type specificity.

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'agonist' and give a specific example from a named sporting action.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for definition: the muscle that contracts to produce a desired movement at a joint (also accept: the prime mover). 1 mark for example: any correct pairing of muscle, movement and sport, e.g. quadriceps (agonist) contract to extend the knee during the kicking phase in football.

knowledge_checks.q: During elbow flexion, which muscle is the agonist?
Which muscle fibre type is best suited to a marathon runner?
When the quadriceps contract to extend the knee, the _____ act as the antagonist.
Type IIx fibres produce explosive power but fatigue rapidly because they rely on _____ energy.
Match each fibre type to its key characteristic:
right: Intermediate, aerobic and anaerobic — team sports

flashcard_questions.q: What is an antagonistic pair of muscles?
flashcard_questions.a: Two muscles producing opposing movements; one contracts while the other relaxes.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the agonist during elbow flexion?
What is the antagonist during knee extension?
flashcard_questions.a: Hamstrings — they relax as the quadriceps contract.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the agonist during ankle plantar-flexion?
What is the agonist during hip flexion in the forward leg swing of running?
Describe Type I muscle fibres in two key properties.
Which fibre type suits a 100 m sprinter, and why?
flashcard_questions.a: Type IIx — fast, powerful, anaerobic, for maximal explosive effort.

flashcard_questions.q: What distinguishes Type IIa fibres from Type IIx?
flashcard_questions.a: Type IIa can use both aerobic and anaerobic energy; Type IIx is purely anaerobic.

flashcard_questions.q: Why do marathon runners have a high proportion of Type I fibres?
flashcard_questions.a: Type I fibres are fatigue-resistant and suit prolonged aerobic activity.

flashcard_questions.q: What sport suits an athlete with mainly Type IIa fibres?
flashcard_questions.a: Middle-distance running or team sports with repeated high-intensity bursts.

flashcard_questions.q: Can training significantly change the ratio of fast to slow twitch fibres?
flashcard_questions.a: No — fibre type ratio is largely genetically determined.

glossary_terms.definition: A pair of muscles that produce opposing movements at the same joint; when one contracts the other relaxes.
The muscle that contracts to produce a desired movement at a joint; also called the prime mover.
The muscle that relaxes and lengthens when its paired agonist contracts, opposing or controlling the movement.
Slow-twitch muscle fibres that are fatigue-resistant, rely on aerobic energy and are suited to endurance activities.
Intermediate fast-twitch muscle fibres that can use both aerobic and anaerobic pathways and suit middle-distance or mixed-intensity activities.
The fastest and most powerful muscle fibres, relying on anaerobic energy, producing explosive force but fatiguing rapidly.
